sections.html:
Martinsburg is the seat of Berkeley County, which fills 321.56 square miles of the Shenandoah Valley in West Virginia's Eastern Panhandle. It forms part of the Hagerstown-Martinsburg metropolitan area, and only Kanawha County has more people among the state's 55 counties.

The county had 122,076 residents in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 139,522 is about 14 percent higher. More people usually means more buyers, but it also means new homes on the market that compete with an older one. Six magisterial districts make up the county: Adam Stephens, Norborne, Potomac, Shenandoah, Tuscarora and Valley.

A few local numbers are worth saving before you list:

  • Berkeley County Commission: 400 W. Stephen St., Martinsburg, 304-264-1923.
  • City of Martinsburg: 232 N. Queen St., 304-264-2131.
  • Sheriff's Tax Office: (304) 264-1982, for balances.
  • County Assessor: 304-264-1904.
  • Eastern Panhandle Organization of Homeowners Associations: 304-728-2201.
  • West Virginia State Tax Department: 800-982-8297.

Does an HOA cover your street? Ask it for a written statement of unpaid dues before closing, since the buyer and the title company will want any balance disclosed. Older houses can carry a local historic designation too. Call the city or county before exterior work or a teardown is on the table.

A quick guide to who does what: the Sheriff's Tax Office answers balance questions. The assessor holds the property record and is the contact for value questions. The County Commission is the body that hears a protest. The State Tax Department, at 800-982-8297, is a further contact for tax questions. Calling the right number first saves a round of transfers when you are short on time.

In this county the assessor decides value and the sheriff handles bills and collection. Every July 1 freezes a parcel's owner, use and worth for the calendar tax year that follows. Four kinds of body levy the tax: county boards of education, county commissions, municipalities and the State.

Parcels are sorted by the constitution into four classes:

  • Class I: intangibles and some farm personal property, currently untaxed.
  • Class II: the owner's own residence used for nothing else, plus farmland in agricultural use.
  • Class III: remaining property located outside any municipality.
  • Class IV: remaining property located inside a municipality.

Suppose an investor buys your house and rents it out. The house leaves Class II, and the tax can shift after the sale.

Protests are heard by the county commission, sitting as the board of equalization and review. The sessions run from February 1 to February 28 at the latest, and you must file before that year's taxes fall due. To prepare:

  • Get proof of value: an independent appraisal or contractor repair estimates both work.
  • Look for errors in the assessor's record on square footage, bedrooms or condition.
  • Ask the assessor's office how filing works. The commission meets at 400 West Stephen Street, Suite 106, Martinsburg.
  • Disputes over classification or taxability may go to the Tax Commissioner (West Virginia Code 11-3-24a), who rules by the end of February.

The state sends a notice when an assessed value rises. A higher number changes what the buyer will owe, so read yours before closing.

Your ticket arrives from the sheriff on or after July 15. Half comes due September 1 and half March 1. A discount rewards paying early. Interest starts when a half goes delinquent, October 1 for the first and April 1 for the second.

December 1 is the last day to apply for the homestead exemption. West Virginia Code 11-6B-3 exempts $20,000 of assessed value, the first slice, for an owner who is 65 or older or certified permanently and totally disabled, and who lived in West Virginia for the two consecutive calendar years before the tax year. Drawing a similar exemption in another state disqualifies you here.

For a balance, phone the Sheriff's Tax Office at (304) 264-1982. The County Assessor's number is 304-264-1904. Confirm any date with the office before you rely on it.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works in Berkeley County
sections.html:
With no buyer's mortgage, the usual West Virginia closing gets simpler. Tell us about the house, review the written offer we send back, and decide. Then an attorney or title company files the deed, pays liens and takes care of tax.

Cash Home Buyers purchases houses as-is. Nothing is charged to the seller in fees, commissions or closing costs, and a declined offer is free.

  • An HOA property with dues unpaid.
  • A rental the landlord is tired of managing.
  • A tax installment that is behind, with interest building.

Each has an obvious first move. For an HOA, request the balance in writing. For taxes, the Sheriff's Tax Office has the figure. For an inherited house, assemble the death certificate and court papers. Nothing here is legal or tax advice. It is general information, so verify specifics with the county office or a qualified professional.

sections.h2: Timeline for listing or selling for cash
sections.html:
Settle the tax picture first, because it touches every later step. Learn the balance and which half it covers. Then collect the HOA statement, if you have an HOA, and any papers an heir will need. After that, choose between listing and a cash sale based on your schedule. Listing means showings, inspection requests and a wait on the buyer's lender. A cash sale means title work and a closing date of your choosing.

On closing day the order is the same either way: liens and taxes are paid first by the title company, and the rest is yours. If the second installment on March 1 or the first on September 1 is close, ask how it will be divided between you and the buyer. Keep the tax ticket and the assessor's notice together in one folder, because the title company may ask for either.

Martinsburg sellers who are weighing the two routes can compare them on the table above: a listing brings commission and seller closing costs, and a cash sale does not. Spend an afternoon on the phone first. One call to the Sheriff's Tax Office, one to the assessor and one to your HOA, if you have one, will tell you most of what a buyer or title company is going to ask. Write down each answer with the date, so the closing agent can see where every figure came from.

faqs.q: Until when can I protest my assessment?
faqs.a: Through February, ahead of the tax due date. The commission opens its board sessions February 1 and closes them by February 28, and a protest filed after that year's taxes are due is too late.

faqs.q: What are the two payment dates?
faqs.a: The first half is due September 1 and the second March 1, once tickets are issued from July 15. Late halves are delinquent after October 1 and April 1 respectively.

faqs.q: Who can claim the $20,000 homestead exemption?
faqs.a: An owner-resident who is 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, with two years of West Virginia residency behind them. File by December 1.

faqs.q: Does my buyer's plan to rent the house change the bill?
faqs.a: Yes. A home lived in by its owner is Class II, whereas a rental goes to Class III or IV based on whether it is inside a municipality.

faqs.q: What will Cash Home Buyers charge me?
faqs.a: Zero. We buy houses in their current condition, and you are billed no fees, commissions or closing costs. Saying no to our offer is free.
